section.title: Woe to the Complacent
section.sectionRationale: Amos turns from the funeral song of chapter five to a scorching woe on the elite of Samaria who feel utterly secure. He paints their luxury in vivid detail, ivory beds, choice meat, improvised music, bowls of wine, finest oils, and then drives home the fatal charge: they are not grieved over the ruin of Joseph. Complacency in the face of a dying nation is itself the sin, and it will send them into exile at the head of the column.
section.thesis: The comfortable self-confidence of those at ease in Zion, feasting while the nation crumbles and caring nothing for its ruin, is not innocence but guilt; God abhors such pride and will hand the secure city over to judgment.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the woe on the complacent who think themselves safe; the luxury of those who will not mourn; and the LORD's oath against Jacob's pride, ending in a nation raised up to oppress them.

units.label: Woe to those at ease
units.note: false security in Zion and Samaria

verses.text: {{hoy|Woe}} to those {{shaanan|at ease}} in Zion and those secure on Mount Samaria, the distinguished ones of the foremost nation, to whom the house of Israel comes.
Cross over to Calneh and see; go from there to the great Hamath; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. Are you better than these kingdoms? Is their territory larger than yours?
You dismiss the day of calamity and bring near a reign of violence.

units.label: The luxury that will not mourn
units.note: ivory beds while Joseph is ruined

verses.text: You lie on beds inlaid with ivory, and lounge upon your couches. You dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall.
You improvise songs on the harp like David and invent your own musical instruments.
You drink wine by the bowlful and anoint yourselves with the finest oils, but you fail to grieve over the {{sheber|ruin}} of Joseph.
Therefore, you will now go into exile as the first of the captives, and your feasting and lounging will come to an end.

units.label: The LORD abhors Jacob's pride
units.note: the sworn oath and the nation raised up

verses.text: The Lord GOD has sworn by Himself, the LORD, the God of Hosts, has declared: “I abhor Jacob’s pride and detest his citadels, so I will deliver up the city and everything in it.”
And if there are ten men left in one house, they too will die.

And when the relative who is to burn the bodies picks them up to remove them from the house, he will call to one inside, “Is anyone else with you?” “None,” that person will answer. “Silence,” the relative will retort, “for the name of the LORD must not be invoked.”
For the LORD gives a command: “The great house will be smashed to pieces, and the small house to rubble.”
“Do horses gallop on the cliffs? Does one plow the sea with oxen? But you have turned {{mishpat|justice}} into poison and the fruit of {{tsedaqah|righteousness}} into wormwood,
you who rejoice in Lo-debar and say, ‘Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?’
For behold, I will raise up a nation against you, O house of Israel,” declares the LORD, the God of Hosts, “and they will oppress you from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah.”

hoy.gloss: An exclamation of woe or alas, the cry raised over the dead at a funeral. Amos hurls it at the living elite of Samaria, pronouncing them as good as buried while they still lounge in luxury. The same word opens the woe on those who long for the Day of the LORD in chapter five; here it falls on those who feel most secure, turning their false peace into a lament.

shaanan.gloss: At ease, secure, untroubled, carefree. The word can describe a healthy peace, but here it names a deadly complacency: a settled confidence that all is well when disaster is at the door. Israel's leaders were relaxed and self-assured, dismissing the day of calamity, and it is precisely this unshaken ease, blind to the nation's ruin, that Amos exposes as sin.

sheber.gloss: A breaking, fracture, shattering, ruin. Joseph, standing for the northern kingdom, is being broken to pieces, yet the elite feast on without a pang of grief. The heart of the indictment is not merely their luxury but their failure to be grieved over the sheber of Joseph; they are unmoved by the very collapse God is bringing, and callousness toward it is itself guilt.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, the right ordering of society especially toward the vulnerable. As in chapter five, Israel has perverted it, here turning mishpat into poison. What should have brought life and protection has been made toxic in the hands of the powerful, a bitter reversal that God will not overlook.

tsedaqah.gloss: Righteousness, right conduct in relationship with God and neighbor. The fruit of righteousness, meant to nourish the community, has been turned into wormwood, a bitter and poisonous plant. Paired again with mishpat, it shows a people who have inverted God's own character, boasting in their own strength while the moral order rots.

basic.context: Amos rounds on the wealthy, self-satisfied leaders of Israel who feel completely safe. He describes their extravagant lifestyle: ivory beds, the best meat, casual music-making, wine drunk by the bowlful, expensive oils. Yet the deadly thing is what they do not do: they are not grieved over the ruin of their own nation. Because they feel secure and care nothing for the coming collapse, they will be the first to be marched off into exile. God swears He detests their pride and will hand the city over.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a woe oracle, a funeral cry pronounced over people who think they are perfectly safe. The point is not that comfort or music or food are wrong in themselves, but that comfort which numbs us to the suffering and coming judgment around us is a grave sin. Complacency is not neutral; it is guilt.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter opens with hoy, woe, the wail raised over the dead, aimed at those who are shaanan, at ease and untroubled. Their crime is that they are not grieved over the sheber, the ruin, of Joseph. And once more they have turned mishpat, justice, into poison and the fruit of tsedaqah, righteousness, into wormwood.
basic.typology: The leaders feast blindly while ruin approaches, a picture answered in reverse by Christ, the true King who wept over a city facing judgment and gave up all comfort to save it. The complacent rich who ignore the day of calamity anticipate the man in Jesus' parable who stored up ease and lost his soul.
basic.christ: Where Israel's rulers lounged in luxury and would not grieve over Joseph's ruin, Jesus is the King who wept over Jerusalem, had nowhere to lay His head, and entered the nation's calamity to bear it Himself. The woe that falls on the complacent is the very judgment Christ absorbed at the cross, so that those who mourn their sin and take refuge in Him find mercy instead of exile.
basic.god: God is not indifferent to how the comfortable treat the collapsing world around them. He swears by Himself that He abhors self-exalting pride and will not let secure sinners feast their way past judgment. Yet the God who tears down the proud citadel is the same God who, in Christ, enters the ruin to rescue.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 6:24-25 pronounces woe on the rich and full who laugh now. Luke 12:16-21 tells of the rich fool at ease. James 5:1-6 warns the self-indulgent rich who ignored the cries of the poor. Luke 19:41-44 shows Christ weeping over a city facing judgment.
basic.oneStory: The complacent feast while the nation dies, and God will not let it stand. The true answer comes in Jesus, the King who refused comfort, wept over the doomed city, and took the woe of judgment upon Himself, so that those who mourn their sin can be spared.

context.literary:
Amos 6 is a single woe oracle stretched over fourteen verses, and it is shaped like a descent. It begins with the loftiest titles in the nation, 'the distinguished ones of the foremost nation,' verse 1, and ends with a foreign power crushing the whole land from end to end, verse 14. The Hebrew for 'foremost,' reshit, comes back in verse 6 for the 'finest' oils, and the idea returns again when the elite go into exile 'as the first of the captives,' verse 7. The first of the nations, with the first of the oils, become the first to be dragged away. The word for nations in verse 1 also comes back in verse 14, in the singular, as the 'nation' the LORD will raise up against them, so that the proud title is answered by an anonymous enemy.

The central section is a catalogue of comfort, verses 4 to 6, and its grammar is part of the point. The sentences pile up as a long line of participles in the Hebrew, lying, sprawling, eating, improvising, drinking, anointing, and the sense is one of endless leisure with no main verb to break it. Then a short, sharp clause cuts across the lines: 'but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph.' The list of pleasures exists so that this sentence can land.

Verses 8 to 14 turn from accusation to sentence, and the style changes with them. Verse 8 is a solemn oath. Verses 9 and 10 are a brief scene with dialogue, the only moment of narrative in the oracle: a relative, a survivor, a hush. Verse 12 is a pair of riddles drawn from farming and travel, the kind of rhetorical questions Amos used elsewhere, as in 3:3-8. Verse 13 quotes the boast of the powerful in their own words, and verse 14 strikes. The chapter thus keeps shifting register, from woe to catalogue to oath to scene to riddle to quotation to verdict, as if no single form could carry the weight of what is being said.
context.historical:
The Israel of Amos's day was enjoying its best years in a century. Jeroboam II had restored the borders 'from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah,' and had recovered Damascus and Hamath, 2 Kings 14:25-28. Assyria was not yet pressing hard, and Aram, the old enemy, was weakened. The wealth that followed was concentrated in Samaria, and excavations there have recovered carved ivory inlays of the kind that decorated royal furniture, which fits the 'beds inlaid with ivory' of verse 4 and the 'houses of ivory' of Amos 3:15. Ahab's palace in the same city had been called an ivory house, 1 Kings 22:39. To the poor, such details were the sign of a class that had stopped looking at the country it ruled.

The meals are as telling as the furniture. Lamb and fattened calf were not daily food; they belonged to feasts and sacrifices. The 'bowls' from which they drank are a word elsewhere used for the basins of the sanctuary, as in Numbers 7:13, and the feast of verse 7 is called a marzeach, a word that appears in Jeremiah 16:5 for a funeral meal. Whatever the exact kind of gathering, the picture is of a banqueting culture that used the vessels and customs of the sacred for pleasure. The music is mentioned with a nod to David, whose instruments were consecrated for praise, 1 Chronicles 23:5 and Nehemiah 12:36, but here the instruments serve the party.

Verse 2 draws on geography. Calneh, the 'great Hamath' and Gath had been prominent cities. Gath had been taken by Hazael of Aram, 2 Kings 12:17, and its walls were later broken down by Uzziah, 2 Chronicles 26:6. Calno and Hamath appear among the cities Assyria later boasted of conquering, Isaiah 10:9. Amos's hearers could look at these places and see what happens to strong cities.

The boast of verse 13 is military. Lo-debar and Karnaim were towns east of the Jordan whose capture the people were boasting of, and the footnotes tell us the names mean 'nothing' and 'horn,' the latter a symbol of strength. The people were pleased with their 'horn,' but they were celebrating a place called 'nothing.' Finally, the territory in verse 14, 'from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah,' matches the boundary Jeroboam had restored in 2 Kings 14:25. The oppression would fall on exactly the land of which they were proudest.
context.canonical:
The woe is a favourite form of the prophets, and Amos 6 belongs with the series in Isaiah 5:8-23, where the same accusations appear: those who add house to house, those who 'rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink,' whose feasts have 'the lyre and harp, tambourines and flutes and wine,' yet 'fail to see the work of His hands,' Isaiah 5:11-12. Isaiah 32:9-11 speaks to 'complacent women' and 'ladies of leisure' who will tremble when the harvest fails, and Zephaniah 1:12 pictures the LORD searching Jerusalem 'with lamps' for the men 'settled in complacency' who say the LORD will do nothing. Ezekiel 16:49 names the sin of Sodom with a phrase that could stand over Amos 6: 'arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy.'

The oath of verse 8 belongs to a thread through the book, since the LORD also swears by His holiness in Amos 4:2 and by the 'Pride of Jacob' in Amos 8:7. Hebrews 6:13 observes that when God made His promise to Abraham 'He swore by Himself,' Genesis 22:16, and so the phrase of Amos 6:8 is a dark mirror of the oath that guaranteed blessing.

The exile that Amos foretells comes in stages. Tiglath-pileser takes captives from Galilee and Gilead, 2 Kings 15:29, and later the king of Assyria captures Samaria and carries the Israelites away, 2 Kings 17:5-6. In the New Testament Jesus draws on the same tradition: 'woe to you who are rich... woe to you who are well fed now,' Luke 6:24-25, and the parable of the rich man and Lazarus in Luke 16:19-31, where a man in purple and fine linen who 'lived each day in joyous splendor' ignored a beggar at his gate. James 5:1-6 addresses rich people who 'lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence,' and the risen Lord's letter to Laodicea quotes the voice of such comfort, 'I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing,' Revelation 3:17. Paul's warning about those who say 'Peace and security' while sudden destruction approaches, 1 Thessalonians 5:3, is the same note struck again.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Amos wanted the powerful to see themselves from outside. The leaders of Samaria believed that their position proved God's favour, for they were the 'distinguished ones' to whom the nation came. By sending them to look at Calneh, Hamath and Gath, he forces a comparison: those cities were large and strong, and they are not now. Security is not a possession but a fragile gift.

He also meant to change what counts as sin. A reader might expect the charge to be violence or theft, and some of that is in the oracle, verse 12 and verse 3. But the sentence that carries the weight is about an absence: 'you fail to grieve.' Amos is saying that to be unmoved by the collapse of one's own people is itself a form of wickedness, and it is the one that prepares the way for the others. A ruling class that can feast through a crisis has already abandoned the people it is meant to serve.

His final aim was to break the boasts. The people spoke of their conquests as achieved 'by our own strength,' verse 13. Amos answers that the LORD, the God of Hosts, is the one who raises nations, so that the same power that had enlarged their borders would now close in on them. For those who would read the book after the exile, the chapter explained that the fall had been a reply to pride and not the failure of God's power.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 4 to 6 describe a way of life, and they must be read with care. Beds, lamb, music, wine and oil are not prohibited anywhere in the passage, and Scripture elsewhere gives all of them as gifts. The charge is that these people have made comfort their whole world and have nothing left for the sufferers around them. The prescription that follows from the passage is therefore not poverty as such but a heart that is grieved over the ruin of others. It asks whether we are the kind of people who can lie on our couches while the country falls apart.

The judgment on the wealthy is the description of what happened in 722 BC and not a general law that comfort leads to exile. But the principle behind it is not time-bound. Ezekiel traces Sodom's guilt to being 'arrogant, overfed, and complacent' while the poor went unhelped, Ezekiel 16:49, and Jesus makes care for the hungry, naked and imprisoned the test of the final judgment, Matthew 25:41-45. Verses 9 and 10, the scene of the survivors, are a record of horror and are not a pattern for how to treat the dead or the dying. They describe what judgment looks like when it falls.

debates.question: What was the marzeach of verse 7?

views.label: A funeral banquet
views.case: Jeremiah 16:5 uses the word for a house of mourning where a 'funeral meal' is held, and some ancient evidence points to such gatherings including heavy drinking. If so, Amos's irony is bitter: the elite are already holding the nation's wake, feasting and lounging at its funeral without knowing it.

views.label: A club of revellers
views.case: Others see a general term for a drinking association or banquet whose members lounged and drank together, with no necessary link to death. The 'feasting and lounging' of verse 7 would then simply describe the aristocratic parties of Samaria, which will end in exile.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is right, the verse says that the party ends. Even if the exact nature of the gathering is uncertain, its place in the oracle is clear: the feasting of the privileged is the first thing the exile will take away.

debates.question: What is happening in the scene of verses 9 and 10?

views.label: Plague and the disposal of bodies
views.case: The 'relative who is to burn the bodies' suggests the aftermath of a disease or siege so severe that bodies must be gathered quickly. Amos 4:10 speaks of plagues 'like those of Egypt,' and burning was unusual enough to be mentioned, as when the men of Jabesh burned the bodies of Saul and his sons, 1 Samuel 31:12.

views.label: A funeral fire to honour the dead
views.case: The BSB footnote offers 'to make a funeral fire to honor the dead.' On this reading the family is performing a final rite, and the horror of the scene is that no one is left to mourn in the usual way.

views.label: The silence of terror
views.case: The hushed reply, 'Silence, for the name of the LORD must not be invoked,' is read in two ways. One is that the survivors are afraid that mentioning the LORD will draw another blow, and so the people who once boasted of His presence now dread His name. The other is that they have given up prayer. Amos 8:3 pictures a similar hush, with corpses strewn 'in silence everywhere.'

debates.bearing: Either way, the scene shows a household emptied and a people unable to speak the name that they had used so freely in the good times. The God they presumed upon is now the one they cannot mention.

debates.question: Why does verse 1 name Zion as well as Samaria?

views.label: Amos addresses both kingdoms
views.case: Amos came from Tekoa in Judah and addresses Israel, but he also condemned Judah in Amos 2:4-5. Judah too had its comfortable leaders, so 'Zion' may be original and Amos may include them in the woe, as Hosea 5:5 says even Judah stumbles.

views.label: A later Judean application
views.case: Some scholars think that the mention of Zion reflects a later reading of the oracle in Judah after Samaria had fallen, applying a warning that had been addressed to the north to the south as well.

debates.bearing: The word does not change the main thrust. It does show that the book was heard, and preserved, as a message for all God's people, not merely for the northern kingdom.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 introduces its target as reshit hagoyim, 'the foremost of the nations.' The word reshit means first, in time or in rank, and it is the same word as the 'finest' oils in verse 6 and is close to the word for 'head' in the phrase for 'first of the captives' in verse 7, where Amos says they will go into exile berosh golim, 'at the head of the exiles.' The Hebrew sets a sequence in motion: first among nations, first in oils, first into captivity. It is hard to hear in English, but a Hebrew listener would have caught the drumbeat.

The verb in the final clause of verse 6, 'you fail to grieve,' comes from a root that means to be sick or weak, and the sense here is that they are not made sick at heart over Joseph's ruin. The grief that should have affected their bodies, their appetite, their sleep, has not touched them at all. The word 'ruin' there, sheber, means a break or fracture, so the picture is of a body in which one part has been shattered and the rest feels nothing, the opposite of Paul's picture in 1 Corinthians 12:26.

In verse 3 the Hebrew says they bring near 'the seat of violence,' with a word for seat that comes from the verb to sit. The elite push the day of calamity away, and in doing so they pull violence close and make it their throne. The 'reign of violence' of the BSB translates a literal image of a throne room: their own rule is the seat from which oppression is exercised.

The word for the 'bowls' of verse 6, mizraq, is used elsewhere for sanctuary basins, as in Numbers 7:13, where silver bowls are offered at the dedication. The nobles drink from vessels named like those of the altar, and the wine is poured in quantity: wine drunk 'by the bowlful.'

In verse 12 the pair 'poison' and 'wormwood,' rosh and laanah, appear together in Deuteronomy 29:18, where the 'root that bears such poisonous and bitter fruit' stands for a heart turned away from the LORD. The prophet picks up that old covenant pairing and says justice has been turned into it. The riddle that precedes, whether horses gallop on cliffs or oxen plow the sea, depends on a textual point the BSB footnote shows: the Hebrew literally asks 'Does one plow (there)?' and the English 'sea' comes from reading the consonants with a different division. Either way, the questions are absurd on purpose, and the answer is no. Justice does not grow in that soil.

The names in verse 13 are puns. Lo-debar means 'no thing' or 'nothing,' and Karnaim means 'horns,' as the footnotes say. Amos has them rejoice in 'Nothing' and ask whether they did not take 'Horns' by their own strength. The same deflating trick appears elsewhere in the book, and it is typical of Amos that he lets the very names of their victories mock them.

Finally, the oath in verse 8, 'sworn by Himself,' literally uses the word for the self or soul of God, nefesh. Amos 8:7 swears by the 'Pride of Jacob,' the same phrase as 'Jacob's pride' in 6:8, and interpreters have disagreed whether the phrase names the arrogance God loathes or God Himself as Israel's true glory.

typology.type: Beds inlaid with ivory and the King with nowhere to lay His head, Amos 6:4
typology.fulfillment: The leaders of Samaria lounge on carved ivory while the nation decays. Jesus meets the same world from the opposite end: 'the Son of Man has no place to lay His head,' Matthew 8:20. Paul gives the pattern its reach: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, and Philippians 2:5-8 describes One who did not grasp equality with God but 'emptied Himself.' The contrast is a deliberate inversion, though it is not a prediction, and the type falls short in that Amos's lounging elite chose their comfort, while Christ's poverty was chosen for others.

typology.type: The grief that is missing, Amos 6:6
typology.fulfillment: Amos accuses the leaders of not being sickened by their people's ruin. In Jesus the grief is present. He 'wept over' Jerusalem as He approached it, Luke 19:41-44, wept at the tomb of Lazarus, John 11:35, and was 'a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief,' Isaiah 53:3. He fulfils the role that Israel's rulers abandoned, a king who feels what his people feel. The correspondence is not simply emotional: He carries the ruin, as Hebrews 4:15 says He sympathises with weakness, which no earthly ruler could do.

In Scripture Joseph is first a brother thrown into a pit while his brothers 'sat down to eat a meal,' Genesis 37:23-25. Amos's picture of leaders feasting while the people of Joseph perish has been heard as an echo of that scene, though the prophet does not draw the connection himself. Joseph is later exalted and saves the very brothers who rejected him, and the New Testament sees in Jesus a greater figure, rejected by His own and yet saving them, Acts 7:9-13. The type is limited: Joseph's story illuminates but never replaces Christ's.

The LORD swears 'by Himself' that He will deliver up the city. The same act, swearing by Himself, secured the promise to Abraham, Genesis 22:16, and Hebrews 6:13-18 says God did so 'by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie.' The oath that confirmed a blessing in Abraham and the oath that confirmed a sentence on Samaria are the same kind of oath. In Christ, who bore the sentence, the oath of promise is made good for everyone who has 'fled to take hold of the hope set before us.'

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by contrast. The nobles of Samaria stretch themselves on ivory and do not grieve. The Son of God comes down, empties Himself, takes 'the form of a servant,' and is 'obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:7-8. He has 'no place to lay His head,' Matthew 8:20, and He weeps. The man who weeps at the tomb of Lazarus, John 11:35, and over the city that will reject Him, Luke 19:41-44, is the exact opposite of those who 'fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph.'

It leads to Christ by its judgment. The 'woe' pronounced on those at ease is repeated by Jesus in the Sermon on the Plain, 'woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort,' Luke 6:24, and enacted in the story of the rich man and Lazarus, Luke 16:19-31, which reads like a short commentary on Amos 6:4-7. In that story, the beggar who lay at the gate is carried to Abraham's side, and the one who feasted finds that the gap between them is fixed. Jesus applies Amos's principle: the way we treat the suffering at our door is the measure of our hearts.

It leads to Christ by the exile. The leaders go into captivity 'at the head of the exiles,' and the sentence is carried out by a foreign nation. Christ, on the other hand, goes outside the camp. 'Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood,' Hebrews 13:12. Where the proud are driven out for their sin, the Holy One is driven out for the sins of others and bears their disgrace, so that those who come to Him 'outside the camp' are brought into a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

It leads to Christ by the failure of human strength. The boast 'Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?' is the final proof of the heart that has no need of a Saviour. Christ's way is the opposite. 'My power is perfected in weakness' is Paul's lesson from the cross, 2 Corinthians 12:9, and the church is told that God 'chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong,' 1 Corinthians 1:27.

A caution is needed. Amos 6 does not name the Messiah, and the typological links are the New Testament's own wisdom rather than a reading Amos intended. The chapter's task is to expose the heart of comfortable self-reliance and to show how deep the problem runs. Christ answers it by being the king who feels, who comes down, and who bears the ruin that the complacent will not even mourn, and by calling us into a life where grief over others' suffering is the sign that the heart is alive.
study.god:
The oath of verse 8 shows how seriously God takes what is described. He swears 'by Himself,' because there is nothing greater to swear by, as Hebrews 6:13 notes of His promises. Judgment here is not a reflex of anger but a settled decision made with the same solemnity as His covenants. He does not threaten and then hope not to have to follow through; He binds Himself.

He is a God who abhors pride. The Hebrew says He 'abhors' and 'detests,' language of revulsion, and the object is arrogance, the 'pride of Jacob,' together with the citadels in which that pride was housed. Pride in Scripture is not a harmless fault but the posture that says we need no one, not even God. The proud confidence of verse 13, 'by our own strength,' is the clearest form of it, and the LORD answers by naming Himself in verse 14 as 'the LORD, the God of Hosts,' the commander who sends the nation. The people take credit for their victories, and He reminds them that He is the one who raises nations.

He is also the God who notices what we do not feel. The central charge is not a deed but a lack, and the God who sees the heart finds the absence of sorrow as culpable as any act of violence. The same God told the prophets that He is near to the brokenhearted, Psalm 34:18, and His displeasure with the complacent is the other side of His love for the afflicted.

He is just and orderly in the way He judges. The first to enjoy the nation's privileges will be first in exile, and the great house and small house are treated alike, verse 11. There is no loophole for rank. He judges leaders more severely because they were given more to steward, which agrees with the principle Jesus states in Luke 12:48.

He is holy in a way that makes silence in His presence appropriate. The relative in verse 10 cannot speak the LORD's name, and that is the dread of those who had treated His name casually. At the same time, Scripture keeps open a door for those who tremble at His word and who turn, as in Isaiah 66:2.

For worship, the passage asks what we can do with comfort. It does not demand that we give up beds and music and meat, but it requires that we hold them as stewards of a God who is moved by suffering. Worship in its fullest form joins thanks for His gifts with grief and action for those who have none.

crossReferences.note: A near twin of Amos 6:4-6. Isaiah's drinkers have 'the lyre and harp, tambourines and flutes and wine,' yet 'fail to see the work of His hands.' Both prophets say the sin is not enjoyment as such but a revelry that is blind to what God is doing.

Sodom's iniquity was that she and her daughters 'were arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy.' Ezekiel reads the great example of judgment in Genesis as a failure of comfortable people to care, which is the exact charge of Amos 6.

The LORD will search Jerusalem 'with lamps' to punish men 'settled in complacency' who think the LORD will do nothing. It is the same self-assurance as the 'secure' of Amos 6:1, now directed at Judah, and it shows how widely the prophets named the danger.

Jesus pronounces woe on the rich, the well fed and those who laugh now, since they have already received their comfort and will hunger and mourn. It is the Amos oracle given in the voice of the Messiah, with the same reversal of fortunes.

A rich man in purple, who lived 'in joyous splendor,' ignored Lazarus at his gate. The parable depicts the character Amos condemns, and it ends with the line that his brothers 'have Moses and the prophets,' which includes the voice of Amos himself.

The rich man who plans bigger barns and tells himself he has plenty laid up for many years hears 'You fool! This very night your life will be required of you.' His security, like that of Amos 6:1, is shattered by a God he forgot.

James tells the rich to 'weep and wail' because their wealth has rotted and the wages withheld from workers cry out. He says they have lived 'in luxury and self-indulgence' and 'fattened' their hearts for the day of slaughter, which is Amos's picture carried into the church.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and foretells its destruction because it did not recognise the time of its visitation. Where Amos's elite failed to grieve over the ruin of Joseph, the Lord grieves over a city that will not turn to Him.

God says, 'By Myself I have sworn,' and promises blessing to Abraham. This is the oath that Hebrews 6:13 explains. Amos 6:8 uses the same pattern for a sentence, and the contrast reminds readers that God's oaths can promise either blessing or judgment, depending on where people stand.

Jesus suffered outside the city gate to sanctify the people, and believers are called to join Him 'outside the camp.' The leaders of Samaria were driven out for their sin; Christ went out for the sins of others, which changes the meaning of exile for His followers.

This passage records Jeroboam II's military success, including the restoration of the border 'from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah.' It explains both the confidence of Amos 6:1 and 6:13 and the weight of verse 14, which promises oppression over just that stretch of territory.

study.oneStory:
Amos 6 belongs in the long story of what goes wrong when God's gifts are mistaken for guarantees. In Eden, the pair were placed in a good place with every tree, and the first temptation was to grasp the one thing that was withheld. By the days of Amos, Israel had a good land, a king's victories and a full table, and the same mistake was being made on a national scale: the gift had become a possession, and the Giver had been forgotten. The chapter shows that comfort does not cure the heart and may harden it.

The passage answers the question of how a chosen people could be so blind. They had been told they were the 'foremost of the nations,' and they took the title as a status instead of a vocation. Israel was called to be a light, to reflect the justice and mercy of the God who chose her, and the rulers of Samaria had inverted that: nations that should have learned from Israel could learn only from her fall.

It sets up the exile, and with it the pain of the prophets' later books. The 'first of the captives' lead a long line that reaches Babylon and beyond. Yet the story does not end there. Amos will close with a promise to restore David's fallen tent, Amos 9:11, and the prophets that follow imagine a king who will judge the poor with justice and a day when no one will lie on ivory while others suffer.

That king arrives in Jesus, who takes the road the elite refused. He comes down, becomes poor, weeps over the city, and goes outside the camp. He announces woe to the complacent and blessing to those who mourn, and he gives His people a new community in which 'if one part suffers, every part suffers with it,' 1 Corinthians 12:26.

The new creation is the reversal of Amos 6. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, no one reclining at ease while a neighbour starves, and no need for grief because God Himself will wipe away every tear. The feast that ends the story is not the feast of Samaria's elite but the wedding supper of the Lamb, to which the poor and hungry are welcome and where the table is open to all.

quiz.q: What is the fatal charge Amos brings against the comfortable elite of Samaria?

options.text: They feel completely secure and are not grieved over the ruin of their own nation.
options.note: Verse six names the missing thing: no grief over the ruin of Joseph.

options.text: They own furniture and enjoy food and music.
options.note: Comfort itself is not the crime; callous indifference to ruin is.

options.text: They live in luxury while ignoring the coming collapse.
options.note: Right about the luxury and indifference; the sharpest point is their lack of grief over Joseph's ruin.

options.text: They forgot to attend the religious festivals.
options.note: The issue is not missed worship but a heart at ease and unmoved by ruin.

quiz.q: Why does Amos begin the chapter with woe, the same cry raised at a funeral?

options.text: He pronounces the secure elite as good as dead, turning their false peace into a lament.
options.note: The funeral cry falls on those who feel most safe.

options.text: Because someone in Samaria had actually died.
options.note: The woe is a prophetic verdict, not a report of a literal funeral.

options.text: Because judgment is coming on the complacent.
options.note: True, and the funeral overtone shows they are already reckoned dead in their security.

options.text: Because Amos was in a gloomy mood.
options.note: The woe is a deliberate prophetic form, not a personal mood.

quiz.q: What does God swear about Jacob's pride?

options.text: He abhors their pride and their fortified citadels and will deliver the city over to judgment.
options.note: God takes the strongest oath, by Himself, against their self-exalting pride.

options.text: He is impressed by their strength and secure cities.
options.note: God detests, not admires, their pride and citadels.

options.text: He is displeased with their arrogance.
options.note: Right, and He binds it to a solemn oath to hand the city over.

options.text: He will overlook it because they are His people.
options.note: Being His people does not shield the proud; He swears against them.

quiz.q: How does the complacency Amos condemns point us to Christ?

options.text: Where they lounged and would not grieve, Jesus refused comfort, wept over the doomed city, and bore its woe.
options.note: Christ is the opposite of the callous elite and the One who takes their woe.

options.text: It simply teaches us to give away our furniture.
options.note: A possible application, but it misses that Christ Himself answers the woe.

options.text: It shows that Jesus also warned against greed.
options.note: True that He warned of it, but the deeper link is that He bore the woe for us.

options.text: It has no connection to Jesus.
options.note: Christ weeping over the city and bearing judgment directly answers this passage.

quiz.q: What warning does Amos 6 hold for people who feel spiritually secure today?

options.text: Comfort that leaves us unmoved by sin and suffering, and confident apart from God, is deadly, not safe.
options.note: False security blind to ruin is the very danger Amos exposes.

options.text: That we should never rest or enjoy anything.
options.note: Scripture allows rest; it warns against complacency that deadens compassion.

options.text: That feeling at ease is a sign of God's approval.
options.note: Amos shows ease can be the mask over coming judgment.

options.text: That we should stay alert and tender rather than complacent.
options.note: Right direction; the passage roots this in the danger of security apart from God.

questions: Amos condemns those who felt at ease while their nation was in ruin. Where has comfort made you numb to sin or suffering around you?
The elite were not grieved over the ruin of Joseph. What ruin, in your community or the wider world, has God been calling you to grieve rather than ignore?
They boasted in Lo-debar and Karnaim, in their own strength. Where are you quietly trusting your own achievements instead of God?
God swore that He abhors pride. Is there a citadel of self-confidence in your life that you need to surrender to Him?
Jesus wept over a doomed city rather than feasting past its danger. How does His grief reshape the way you respond to a world under judgment?

translationNotes.note: The finest oils translates a phrase for the choicest ointments; the picture is of the elite pampering themselves with premium luxury even as the nation breaks apart.

The relative who is to burn the bodies may also be rendered the one who makes a funeral fire to honor the dead; the grim scene assumes a plague or slaughter so severe that survivors dare not even invoke the name of the LORD.

Lo-debar sounds like the Hebrew for nothing, and Karnaim means horns, a symbol of strength; Amos mocks Israel for boasting that they took a place called Nothing and a place called Strength by their own power.
